entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Victor IV was the antipope from March to May 1138. He rose to power as a papal nominee of the Holy Roman Emperor Lothair III during the Investiture Controversy, which pitted the Catholic Church against the Holy Roman Empire. This period saw significant tensions between the church and secular rulers across Western Europe.

Victor IV's reign was short-lived, lasting only until May 29, 1138, when he was deposed by the conclave of cardinals. The Investiture Controversy ultimately led to a compromise at the Council of Reims in 1129, where the emperor acknowledged the church's right to appoint bishops.

The controversy had far-reaching consequences for European politics and the relationship between church and state. It marked the beginning of the end of imperial authority over ecclesiastical appointments and paved the way for the growth of national kingdoms.

Victor IV's legacy is one of a pivotal moment in medieval history, where the struggle for power and influence played out between two dominant forces: the Catholic Church and the Holy Roman Empire.
